content: This is a discussion thread for #Project announcements > `bubble`, a sandboxing tool for Lean users

How does this compare to using docker containers (one per project) and letting VSCode (VSCodium in my case so no Microsoft telemetry) ssh into it?

Especially for allowing language models to edit and compile code, I find it very important to use a container (maybe one should even use a VM?). So far, docker seemed adequate to me. Is this better?

Adomas Baliuka said:

ssh into it

You don't have to ssh into it, VSCode can attach to containers even without ssh

(Sorry if this is highjacking the thread too much, I didn't intend that. Edited out my questions too late when I looked it up instead of asking, as I should have from the start. It installs a code-server and then runs it with docker exec, no ssh involved.
(you might be confusing it with the Remote SSH extension)

Adomas Baliuka said:

What is the tool/extension called?

"Dev Containers", previously called "Remote Containers"

Adomas Baliuka said:

How does this compare to using docker containers (one per project) and letting VSCode (VSCodium in my case so no Microsoft telemetry) ssh into it?

Yes, it's comparable, but uses open source containerization instead of Docker.

bubble does lots of nice convenience things that otherwise you need to do by hand:

  • sets up the lean toolchain, VSCode server, and the lean4 extension inside the container
  • mounts a globally updated Mathlib cache as read-only + internal overlay updates
  • provides a proxy for Github that ensures your github token never enters the bubble

Kim Morrison said:

uses open source containerization instead of Docker.

What's not open source in Docker? (core, as in the engine and CLI, not the UI called "Docker Desktop" which you don't have to use)
Also, may I recommend podman as an alternative? I've been using it on macOS for a year and loving it

Kim Morrison said:

Running Lean code from untrusted sources is potentially dangerous, just as for any programming language.

I want to humbly ask, with no offense intended, why is trusting bubble better than trusting random Mathlib PRs, especially when most Mathlib PRs are short enough to glance over before cloning to make sure there's no metaprogramming?
bubble is ~25,000 lines of Python, and Claude seems to have written a lot of it.
Can you vouch that the 25k lines, which include running git/incus/colima and touching the user's filesystem, will not under any circumstance do anything destructive to the user's filesystem, even by accident?

Obviously there are choices here:

  • take the time to set up your own sandboxing solution
  • use something off-the-shelf and convenient like this, trusting that other people have thought about it and got it right
  • decide to just accept the risks of running external code and/or YOLO AI agents unsandboxed

And no, of course I don't vouch completely for bubble, or any of my Mathlib PRs, or grind, etc, not doing anything wrong. :-) That trust comes from people using tools, reading the source code (and asking agents to read it for them!).

Malvin Gattinger said:

I am curious what exactly you mean with"mounts a globally updated Mathlib cache as read-only". Is this for the cache as it gets downloaded by lake exe cache get or is it the unpacked version in .lake/packages/mathlib afterwards? If it's the latter then if I understand correctly this would solve the "every project needs 6GB of my disk" problem? :star_struck:

This is completely orthogonal. If you are ready to use the same version of Lean and Mathlib for several projects you can already tell lake to use a single copy of Mathlib. This has nothing to do with sandboxing.
https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/wiki/Project-setup:-globally-shared-mathlib-installation has instructions for that

I knew that other solutions for this exist, but that page for example is quite long and eventually wants me to modify lakefile.lean in all projects where I want to use the shared mathlib, right? To me it sounds like "bubble" then does not need such a modification because it makes the same files appear in multiple folders by mounting.

The trick bubble uses is different from the wiki solution, and serves a slightly different purpose --- and only saves a fraction of the per-checkout cost. (I've corrected my post above.)

bubble doesn't rewrite any lakefiles to use relative paths. Instead, bubble maintains an outside-of-bubble version of each git repository (both for projects you load directly, and their lake dependencies) in ~/.bubble/git/. These are "bare clones", i.e. all the git data is there, but there's no working copy.

Next, inside each bubble (which I'm using to mean "container configured by bubble), we mount the relevant repositories read-only. Then, we setting up the git repositories in .lake/packages/ for each dependency, we create them using a "git alternate" pointing to the mounted read only copy. This means that when git goes looking for data objects, it tries the alternate first, but if it doesn't find it then it just does normal git operations on the read-write repository within the bubble. In normal operations, it writes very little inside the bubble.

This is mostly a time-saving effort, rather than a space-saving effort: it drastically speeds up the time to clone dependencies on subsequent bubble creation.

This doesn't address duplication of .olean files which are copied out of the cache into the .lake/packages/ directory. I intentionally didn't do anything about this because ... we're trying to replace the entire cache system in a way that .olean files won't ever be copied into .lake/packages/, and I thought this would be deployed by now, but it isn't.

The LAKE_ARTIFACT_CACHE=true setting would probably help here, but again, I don't really want to write any code specific to the current caching code when we on the verge of ripping it all out and replacing it.
Isn't olean duplications handed by .lake/package-overrides.json?

Someone really needs to update https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/wiki/Project-setup:-globally-shared-mathlib-installation!

I could try to update them, but it's the first time I hear of package-overrides.json so some reading is needed.

Also, feel free to edit/remove the name at the top. The intention of "written by Jon" was to present it as less official with less guarantee that it's the best solution available.
@Kim Morrison Does bubble support repos where the Lean project is in a subdirectory?

Alexander Bentkamp said:

Kim Morrison Does bubble support repos where the Lean project is in a subdirectory?

No. It determines if it is looking at a lean repo by looking for lean-toolchain in the root.
Seems easy enough to add auto-detection, however: https://github.com/kim-em/bubble/pull/295
Wow, thanks!
It assumes there is only a single lean-toolchain in the repo, is that okay?
Hm, most of my repos have several lean-toolchain files (with identical content).

Okay, kim-em/bubble#296 ('d) allows multiple lean-toolchains. If they disagree, then the bubble is created without any toolchain embedded, and elan will handle retrieving them on demand. (And bubble prints a warning in this situation.)
Great! Thanks a lot!

When I start the bubble, I get:

Multiple Lean projects detected (lean, tests/lean); skipping auto-build. Run `lake build` in your project's subdirectory.

When I run lake build inside the bubble:

$ lake build
error: error during download
info: caused by: [28] Timeout was reached (Failed to connect to github.com port 443 after 132941 ms: Could not connect to server)

Do I need to choose less restrictive network settings than the default?

Snir Broshi said:

Kim Morrison said:

uses open source containerization instead of Docker.

What's not open source in Docker? (core, as in the engine and CLI, not the UI called "Docker Desktop" which you don't have to use)
Also, may I recommend podman as an alternative? I've been using it on macOS for a year and loving it

I see little human reasoning in the choice of Incus to achieve open source containerization. The ecosystem for open-source interoperable with the OCI formats is vast https://opencontainers.org/. The container image format of Incus has been adopted by few (and I suspect no other tools).

I also recommend podman. I have been using podman for around 7 years. For Linux users, this guide to running personal pesistent containers https://cnest.readthedocs.io/ might be useful. It is 100% human authored.

I build OCI (Docker) container images for elan and Lean toolchains at:
https://gitlab.com/ellerman/dock/lean-toolchain/container_registry
https://gitlab.com/ellerman/dock/elan/container_registry
Those links go to both OCI image registries and git repos of the source to building those OCI images (via GitLab CI). These are OCI images that work with any tools that interoperate with OCI images.

Unfortunately I have not yet written documentation for how to use these container images. But I'm more than happy to answer questions, help folks learn how to use OCI containers on Linux (and/or Kubernetes), and coordinate more official OCI images if folks are interested.

I'm not a Windows, Mac, or VSCode user, so I'm not super helpful for those use cases.
